planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; red-veined sorrel tolerates more shade than most leafy greens and is grown as much for its striking dark red leaf veining as for its tart, lemony flavor.

directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Red-veined sorrel produces attractive arrow-shaped green leaves boldly patterned with deep burgundy-red veins, making it as valued for ornamental use in a shaded bed or container as for its tart, lemony flavor in salads and light cooking, used sparingly like common sorrel. It tolerates more shade than most leafy greens, making it a useful edible for the partly shaded edge of a garden bed, and it self-seeds readily once established, which can make it a semi-permanent presence if seed heads are not removed. Harvest young leaves regularly for the mildest flavor and best appearance, since older leaves become tougher and more sour.

common_name: Summerific Hardy Hibiscus (Compact Large-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus Series)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Summerific series hibiscus were bred for a more compact, well-branched habit than older hardy hibiscus, which tend to grow tall and leggy, while still producing dinner-plate-sized flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. The Summerific breeding series was developed to bring the enormous, dinner-plate-sized flowers of hardy hibiscus into a shorter, sturdier, more floriferous plant than older cultivars, which often grow tall, sparse, and prone to flopping. Depending on the specific cultivar in the series, flower colors range from pure white and soft pink to deep red and near-black-leaved forms, all blooming from midsummer into fall. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown, and it is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil.

common_name: Kopper King Hardy Hibiscus (Bronze-Leaved Pink-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Kopper King is valued for its coppery-bronze foliage, an unusual contrast to the huge pale pink, red-eyed flowers, and it dies back completely to the ground each winter, emerging late in spring.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season. Kopper King is a striking hardy hibiscus hybrid combining bold, dinner-plate-sized, pale pink flowers with a deep red central eye against dramatic bronze-copper foliage, a foliage color unusual among hardy hibiscus cultivars that makes the plant a strong focal point even before it flowers. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, often causing gardeners to worry it has died, so mark its location and be patient. It flowers from midsummer into fall on a large, robust, well-branched plant, and is generally pest-free and easy to grow given consistently moist soil.

common_name: Miss Huff Lantana (Cold-Hardy Tall Orange-Pink Lantana)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Miss Huff is notably more cold-hardy than most lantana cultivars, often returning reliably from the roots after winters that kill other lantana to the ground or outright.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Miss Huff is one of the most widely planted lantana cultivars in the Gulf South, valued for a rare combination of vigorous, tall growth, months of nonstop orange-to-pink multicolor flower clusters that draw butterflies in large numbers, and notably better cold tolerance than most lantana, regularly surviving winters as a root-hardy perennial where less hardy cultivars are killed outright. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil with ease once established, needing only an annual hard cutback in late winter after the coldest weather has passed to remove winter-killed top growth and encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; Sapphire Showers has a more trailing, cascading habit than upright duranta cultivars, making it well suited to hanging baskets, containers, and spilling over walls.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Sapphire Showers is a trailing form of duranta, producing cascading stems draped in clusters of small, tubular blue-violet flowers over a long warm-season bloom period that draws butterflies and hummingbirds. Its spreading, arching habit sets it apart from the more upright, tree-like duranta cultivars often grown as small specimen trees, making it a good choice for hanging baskets, raised containers, or spilling over a low wall. In zone 9a it typically dies back to the ground after a hard freeze but regrows quickly from the roots the following spring in most winters; in colder zones it is best grown as a container annual or overwintered indoors.
